Chapter 7: The Influence of Environment—Shaping Spaces for Success.
You know, it's easy to think that self-control is all about grit and determination. But have you ever noticed how much your surroundings really shape your choices?
Sure, personal effort matters a lot, but the environment you’re in—the spaces you spend time in, the little cues you see, and even the people around you—all have a huge impact on how easy or tough it is to stick to your goals.
Instead of just relying on willpower, what if you could design your environment to make good decisions almost automatic?
That’s the idea behind what’s called choice architecture. Basically, it means making small, thoughtful tweaks to your surroundings that gently nudge your behavior in a positive direction.
For example, imagine you want to eat healthier. If you keep fresh fruit or nuts right at eye level and tuck the candy out of sight, you’re far more likely to reach for the better option. Or, if you organize your workspace to cut down on distractions—maybe by silencing your phone, or keeping only what you need on your desk—you’ll find it’s a lot easier to focus and get things done.
There are a few simple ways you can shape an environment that truly supports your goals:
Try removing temptations you know you struggle with—like keeping junk food out of the house, or turning off those never-ending notifications while you work.
Set up physical reminders of your goals. Sticky notes, vision boards, or daily checklists can help keep your intentions front and center.
And, pay attention to your natural rhythms. If you’re a morning person, schedule your toughest tasks for those early hours, when your energy and willpower are at their peak.
The people in your life matter, too. Surrounding yourself with folks who support your values or share your goals can make a world of difference.
Sometimes, even small changes—like joining a walking group or working alongside focused friends—can make self-control feel less like a solo struggle, and more like something you do together.
Picture someone who wants to read more. By putting a good book on their nightstand and stashing the TV remote in another room, they’re setting up their environment to gently encourage reading instead of mindless channel surfing.
Over time, these little tweaks really add up, making it so much easier to stick to what you want to do.
So, here’s the key takeaway: willpower isn’t just about what’s going on inside you—it’s also about the dance you do with the world around you.
By shaping your spaces to support the choices you want to make, you save your willpower for when you need it most—and following through on your intentions becomes a whole lot more natural.
